subject: Chemistry
topic: Moles, titration ratios, gases and formula determination
scope: A-Level untiered quantitative teaching. Includes calculations and method evaluation, but not supervised completion of required practical 1 or complete treatment of every yield and atom-economy application. Original teaching and practice, not official examination material. Practice rubrics are for self-review. This topic does not establish whole-course coverage, independent subject review or publication approval.
prerequisites: Convert cubic centimetres, cubic decimetres and cubic metres.
objectives: Connect particle number, mass, amount and concentration.
Use reaction ratios rather than equating unrelated amounts.
Apply appropriate units and evaluate measurement limitations.

notes.heading: Amounts are counts, not masses
paragraphs: A mole contains the Avogadro number of specified entities. Name those entities: one mole of oxygen molecules contains two moles of oxygen atoms. Amount n = m/M uses mass in grams with molar mass in grams per mole. Relative formula mass itself has no unit; molar mass does. The same mass of two substances generally contains different amounts because their molar masses differ. Retain extra digits during working and round the final result to a precision justified by the data.

notes.heading: Solutions and reaction ratios
paragraphs: For concentration c in mol dm^-3, n = cV requires V in dm^3. Divide a volume in cm^3 by 1000. A balanced equation supplies mole ratios, not mass ratios. In H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O, one mole of acid reacts with two of sodium hydroxide. First find a measured reagent’s amount, apply the stoichiometric ratio, and only then calculate the unknown concentration. A limiting reactant is the one supplying the smallest amount divided by its equation coefficient.

notes.heading: Gas and formula reasoning
paragraphs: In pV = nRT, use pressure in pascals, volume in cubic metres and temperature in kelvin with R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1. A room-temperature molar-volume shortcut is not valid for arbitrary pressure and temperature. Real gases depart from ideal behaviour, especially where intermolecular attractions or particle volume matter.

An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number atom ratio. Convert each element’s mass to amount before dividing by the smallest amount. Ratios such as 1:1.5 need multiplication by two, not careless rounding. Divide molecular mass by empirical-formula mass to obtain the integer multiplier for a molecular formula.

notes.heading: Titration quality
paragraphs: Prepare a standard solution by quantitative transfer into a volumetric flask, rinse transferred material into it, dissolve fully and make up to the mark with the meniscus read at eye level. Mix thoroughly. Rinse the pipette with the solution it will deliver and the burette with its titrant; residual water there dilutes measured solutions. Distilled water added to the conical flask changes volume but not the amount originally pipetted. Use concordant titres, excluding the rough titre; do not conceal a poor spread by averaging everything. A titre is the difference between two readings, so both contribute to uncertainty.

workedExamples.prompt: 25.0 cm^3 of H2SO4 needs 20.0 cm^3 of 0.100 mol dm^-3 NaOH. Find acid concentration.
steps: Acid amount = 0.00100 mol; divide by 0.0250 dm^3.

workedExamples.prompt: A compound is 40.0% C, 6.67% H, 53.33% O by mass. Use Ar C=12, H=1, O=16.
steps: On a 100 g basis, amounts are about 3.333, 6.67 and 3.333 mol.

misconceptions.claim: Equal solution volumes contain equal moles.
Adding water to the conical flask changes the titre needed.
misconceptions.correction: It does not change the amount pipetted, provided no analyte is lost and the same endpoint chemistry applies.

flashcards.front: How do mass and amount connect?
flashcards.back: n = m/M with consistent mass units.

flashcards.front: What units does pV = nRT need here?

flashcards.back: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.

flashcards.front: Why rinse the burette with titrant?
flashcards.back: To prevent residual water diluting it.

questions.prompt: [A-Level: untiered] Find the amount in 5.85 g NaCl using molar mass 58.5 g mol^-1.
[A-Level: untiered] 25.0 cm^3 sulfuric acid reacts with 30.0 cm^3 of 0.200 mol dm^-3 NaOH. Use H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O to find acid concentration.
solution: NaOH amount = 0.00600 mol; acid amount = 0.00300 mol.

questions.prompt: [A-Level: untiered] Calculate the volume of 0.500 mol ideal gas at 300 K and 100000 Pa, R=8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1.
[A-Level: untiered] A compound has empirical formula CH2O and molecular mass 180. Use Ar C=12, H=1, O=16. Find its molecular formula.
[A-Level: untiered] Each burette reading has uncertainty ±0.05 cm^3. Estimate the maximum percentage uncertainty in a 20.00 cm^3 titre.
solution: Two readings give a maximum uncertainty of ±0.10 cm^3.

questions.prompt: [A-Level: untiered] Explain why rinsing a conical flask with distilled water is acceptable but leaving water in a burette before adding titrant is problematic.
questions.answer: Flask water preserves analyte amount; burette water reduces titrant concentration.
solution: The measured analyte is already present in a fixed amount.
Dilution in the burette changes moles delivered per measured volume.

teachingSequence.title: Build the explanation
teachingSequence.guidance: Read the opening sections. Reconstruct the reasoning in worked example 1, then attempt the first two questions before looking at their answers.

teachingSequence.title: Apply and distinguish
teachingSequence.guidance: Study the remaining sections and worked example 2. Explain why its reasoning fits this situation. Check the programme and tier labels before attempting the next questions.

teachingSequence.title: Test and revise
teachingSequence.guidance: Attempt the remaining questions from memory. Compare each claim with the practice marking points, correcting unsupported reasoning. These are self-review tasks, not automated exam grades.

revisionGuide.summary: Convert units, calculate an amount, apply the equation ratio, then find the requested quantity. Measurement quality is part of the chemical argument.
keyIdeas: How do mass and amount connect? n = m/M with consistent mass units.
What gives reacting mole ratios? Coefficients in the balanced equation.
What units does pV = nRT need here? Pa, m^3, mol and K.
What is an empirical formula? The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
Why rinse the burette with titrant? To prevent residual water diluting it.
